# Implement block: Scratch Ticket (SwiftUI)

You are adding the "Scratch Ticket" block from Native Cook to the user's iOS app. The block already exists as working SwiftUI code. Your job is to bring it into this project faithfully, not to write a new one that looks similar.

## The block

A scratch-off lottery ticket lying on a dark green table: cream card stock with a printed dashed frame, a sunflower mark, the title "Lucky Bloom" and a tear-off stub joined by a row of punched holes, its prize line hidden and a barcode beside it. The middle is a window of holographic foil, brushed silver with a fine diamond guilloché, soft iridescent bands, a drifting sheen and twinkling four-point sparkles, with a sunflower and "Scratch to reveal" pressed into it. A finger rubs the foil away along a soft round brush, shedding little foil flakes that tumble down the screen; once enough is cleared the rest dissolves with a hot golden edge, the sunflower photo underneath settles into place, the stub prints the prize and confetti bursts. "New ticket", or throwing the ticket off to the left, deals the next one in from the right.

**Motion.** Scratching draws the finger's path as one curve through the midpoints of its samples (taken every 2.5 pt or more), stroked 46 pt wide with round caps and a 5 pt blur, erasing the foil with a destination-out blend inside the foil's own layer. The window is split into a 16 × 12 grid; a cell is cleared when the brush's middle (0.45 of its width) passes over it, checked every 6 pt along each segment, and at 60% of the cells the ticket is revealed. Every 7 pt of fresh foil tears off one to five flakes (2–5.5 pt, life 0.9–1.6 s) thrown with 12% of the finger's velocity plus up to 200 pt/s upwards, falling at 1300 pt/s² with a drag of 2.6/s, spinning and flipping, drawn with the same foil shader. The reveal dissolves the remaining foil along a noise field over 1.1 s on a cubic-bezier(0.33, 0, 0.2, 1), its edge glowing gold; the photo eases from 110% to 100% with it, the ticket bumps 3.5% in 140 ms and springs back (600 ms, damping ratio 0.45), 110 confetti pieces in five colours burst upwards at 420–1140 pt/s (gravity 1150 pt/s², drag 1.8/s, life 1.5–2.4 s), the prize springs up into the stub, the "New ticket" pill fills cream over 300 ms and a success haptic fires. The foil's sheen follows the finger while scratching (easing at 6/s) and otherwise drifts once per 9 s. Dealing: the new ticket springs in from 115% of the screen's width (800 ms, damping ratio 0.8) while the old one is thrown left to 125% (650 ms, damping ratio 1, carrying the release velocity), each tilting up to 9° with its travel; a light haptic marks a deal. Outside the foil the ticket can be dragged: left it follows the finger and is thrown past 30% of the width or 800 pt/s, right it gives a 70 pt rubber band, and otherwise it springs back (450 ms, damping ratio 0.8) with the release velocity. autoPlay loops every 9 s from a fresh ticket: a virtual fingertip touches down at 0.7 s and scratches a seven-leg zigzag down the foil until 3.9 s, lifting as soon as the ticket is revealed; "New ticket" presses at 6.5 s and the next ticket rests from about 7.3 s. Every fresh ticket looks the same until scratched and the foil's motion repeats every 9 s, so one period loops cleanly; a touch pauses the loop for 4 s, then it deals a fresh ticket if needed and starts over. Reduced motion keeps the scratching and the dissolve, drops the flakes, the confetti, the photo zoom and the bump, and crossfades tickets over 320 ms instead of sliding them. On Android 12 and older, which cannot run the foil shader, the foil and its flakes are a silver-rainbow gradient that slides with the light and fades out as it dissolves.

## Reference source

The block is built and running in the Native Cook source repository. Each link below is a file on GitHub. To read one as plain text, replace `https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/` with `https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/` in its address.

### Demo (start here)

- [ScratchTicketDemo.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/ScratchTicket/ScratchTicketDemo.swift)

### Files of the block

- [ScratchTicket.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/ScratchTicket/ScratchTicket.swift)
- [ScratchTicketCard.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/ScratchTicket/ScratchTicketCard.swift)
- [ScratchTicketEngine.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/ScratchTicket/ScratchTicketEngine.swift)
- [ScratchTicketFoil.metal](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Blocks/Gestures/ScratchTicket/ScratchTicketFoil.metal)

### Shared helpers the block uses

- [swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift](https://github.com/Native-Cook/native-cook/blob/main/swift/NativeCook/Shared/ComponentSupport.swift)

### Frameworks

It needs no framework beyond SwiftUI.

## Your instructions

_Anything specific to this app goes here: where the block should appear, what to rename, what to change. Left empty, integrate the block as it is._

## How to work

Work like an experienced iOS engineer joining an existing project: learn the app first, read only what you need, decide early how the block fits, then integrate it with as little disruption as possible. Take the steps in order.

**Done means** the block is reachable in the user's app and behaves like the reference in the iOS Simulator or on a device. A SwiftUI preview is useful while you work, but it is not the proof: build and run the app.

**Fidelity.** Bring over the real implementation. Keep its structure, colours, sizes, timings and curves. Change only what this project requires and what "Your instructions" ask for.

If you already learned this project earlier in the conversation, reuse what you know and skip step 2. Learn it again only if the project changed or something you need is missing.

### 1. Check where you are

- You need the project's files and a terminal. If this prompt was pasted into a chat that has neither, stop and say so: it has to be run by a coding agent opened on the project.
- Confirm the project is an iOS app built with Xcode (an `.xcodeproj`, an `.xcworkspace` or a Swift package with an app target). If it is something else, stop, say what you found, and do not create a new app inside it unless the instructions ask for one.

### 2. Learn the host app

- The app target, its deployment target and its Swift version.
- SwiftUI, UIKit or both, and how a screen is shown today: `NavigationStack`, a coordinator, a tab bar, a storyboard.
- How files join the target: a folder the project synchronises, or a file list in the project that you have to extend.
- Conventions: folder layout, naming, where colours, fonts and assets live.
- Type names the app already uses, so the block's types do not collide with them.

### 3. Read the block

- Swift files in a module do not import each other, so the demo alone will not lead you to the rest. The list above names every file of the block: read them all.
- The demo is how the source repository shows the block. Bring over what the demo shows, not the repository's gallery. Anything listed under "Used by the demo only" stays behind.
- Read the block's initialiser and its defaults. The demo may switch on an option that makes the block play by itself for a recording (for example `autoPlay`). Keep the option; leave it off in the user's app unless asked.

### 4. Decide the fit

- The source app targets iOS 17. If the host targets an older system, check each API the block uses and tell the user what would have to change before you lower anything. Do not raise the host's deployment target without asking.
- If a type or function name of the block already exists in the app, rename the block's one, in every file that uses it, and say that you did.
- Shared helpers: copy the ones the block uses next to it, or fold them into the block's files. Do not copy helpers it never calls.
- In a UIKit app, show the block through a `UIHostingController`.

### 5. Bring it in

- Add the block's files to the app target, keeping their names.
- Copy its asset catalogs, loose resources and fonts, and check that the names the code asks for match the names in the bundle: a wrong name compiles and then shows nothing.
- A `.metal` file has to be compiled into the same target as the code that calls its function.
- Keep reduced-motion handling, haptics and accessibility labels as they are in the source.
- Mount the block where the instructions say. With no instructions, add a screen named after the block and make it reachable the way the app's other screens are.

### 6. Run it

- Build the app target for a simulator with `xcodebuild` or the project's own script, and fix every error and new warning the block introduced.
- Run it and use the block: every state, every gesture, light and dark appearance if the block follows them, and once with Reduce Motion on.
- If the build or the simulator fails for a reason outside the block, report the error and ask how to continue.

### 7. Report

- Files added and changed, and anything renamed to avoid a collision.
- How to reach the block in the app.
- Anything that differs from the reference, and why.
